segments.text: Same juice bottles, same score of minus two. The z-test says reject. The t-test says don't.
segments.caption: Same juice bottles, same score of -2. The z-test says reject. The t-test says don't.

segments.text: So who's right? Here's z-test versus t-test, the complete comparison. Save this one!
segments.caption: So who's right? Here's z-test versus t-test, the complete comparison. Save this one!

segments.text: Here are the textbook definitions.
segments.caption: Here are the textbook definitions.

segments.text: A z-test compares a sample mean with a population mean, when the population standard deviation is known.
segments.caption: A z-test compares a sample mean with a population mean, when the population standard deviation is known.

segments.text: A t-test does the same, when it's unknown and has to be estimated from the sample.
segments.caption: A t-test does the same, when it's unknown and has to be estimated from the sample.

segments.text: The formulas differ by one letter.
segments.caption: The formulas differ by one letter.

segments.text: z divides by sigma, the true population spread. t divides by s, the spread estimated from the sample.
segments.caption: z divides by sigma, the true population spread. t divides by s, the spread estimated from the sample.

segments.text: An estimate adds extra uncertainty, especially when the sample is small.
segments.caption: An estimate adds extra uncertainty, especially when the sample is small.

segments.text: That's why the t curve has fatter tails.
segments.caption: That's why the t curve has fatter tails.

segments.text: With two degrees of freedom, the tails are very fat. With five, thinner. By thirty, t is almost the normal curve.
segments.caption: With 2 degrees of freedom, the tails are very fat. With 5, thinner. By 30, t is almost the normal curve.

segments.text: Degrees of freedom, n minus one, tell you which t curve to use.
segments.caption: Degrees of freedom, n - 1, tell you which t curve to use.

segments.text: Now watch the five percent cut-off shrink as the sample grows.
segments.caption: Now watch the 5% cut-off shrink as the sample grows.

segments.text: Five degrees of freedom: two point five seven one. Ten: two point two two eight. Thirty: two point zero four two. Sixty: exactly two. A hundred: one point nine eight four.
segments.caption: 5 degrees of freedom: 2.571. 10: 2.228. 30: 2.042. 60: exactly 2. 100: 1.984.

segments.text: And with infinite data: one point nine six. The z value. t becomes z.
segments.caption: And with infinite data: 1.96. The z value. t becomes z.

segments.text: Back to our puzzle. A score of minus two only beats the t cut-off with more than sixty degrees of freedom.
segments.caption: Back to our puzzle. A score of -2 only beats the t cut-off with more than 60 degrees of freedom.

segments.text: Nine bottles: fail to reject. A hundred bottles: reject. Both tests were right, for what they knew.
segments.caption: 9 bottles: fail to reject. 100 bottles: reject. Both tests were right, for what they knew.

segments.text: The t-test wasn't wrong. It was more careful, because nine bottles can't pin down the spread.
segments.caption: The t-test wasn't wrong. It was more careful, because 9 bottles can't pin down the spread.

segments.text: So which one should you use? Ask one question: do you know sigma?
segments.caption: So which one should you use? Ask one question: do you know sigma?

segments.text: Yes: z-test. No: t-test, at any sample size. And with a big sample, the two give almost the same answer.
segments.caption: Yes: z-test. No: t-test, at any sample size. And with a big sample, the two give almost the same answer.

segments.text: Interview trap: use z when n is over thirty. That's a rule of thumb, not the definition.
segments.caption: Interview trap: use z when n is over 30. That's a rule of thumb, not the definition.

segments.text: The real question is whether you know sigma. In practice, you rarely do, so t is the default.
segments.caption: The real question is whether you know sigma. In practice, you rarely do, so t is the default.

segments.text: And with a big sample, s gets very close to sigma. That's why z works as an approximation there.
segments.caption: And with a big sample, s gets very close to sigma. That's why z works as an approximation there.

segments.text: So where is the z-test really used? Proportions.
segments.caption: So where is the z-test really used? Proportions.

segments.text: In an A-B test, or a poll, the spread comes from the proportion itself, so we use z. Ten percent versus twelve percent conversion? That's a z-test.
segments.caption: In an A/B test, or a poll, the spread comes from the proportion itself, so we use z. 10% versus 12% conversion? That's a z-test.

segments.text: Its standard error is the square root of p times one minus p, over n. No sigma needed.
segments.caption: Its standard error is the square root of p times 1 - p, over n. No sigma needed.

segments.text: The same cut-offs build confidence intervals: plus or minus one point nine six with z, plus or minus the t value with t.
segments.caption: The same cut-offs build confidence intervals: ±1.96 with z, ±the t value with t.

segments.text: That's why a small-sample t interval is always a little wider.
segments.caption: That's why a small-sample t interval is always a little wider.
